name: String
doc:
A library for string manipulation and verification.

`String` is Robot Framework's standard library for manipulating
strings (e.g. [Replace String Using Regexp], [Split To Lines]) and
verifying their contents (e.g. [Should Be String]).

In addition to strings, most of the keywords work also with bytes.
Bytes support was heavily enhanced in Robot Framework 7.4.

Following keywords from the [BuiltIn] library can also be used with strings
and bytes:

- `Get Length`
- `Length Should Be`
- `Should (Not) Be Empty`
- `Should (Not) Be Equal (As Strings/Integers/Numbers)`
- `Should (Not) Match (Regexp)`
- `Should (Not) Contain`
- `Should (Not) Start With`
- `Should (Not) End With`
- `Convert To String`
- `Convert To Bytes`

[BuiltIn]: https://robotframework.org/robotframework/latest/libraries/BuiltIn.html

keywords.name: Convert To Lower Case
keywords.doc:
Converts string to lower case.

Uses Python's standard
[str.lower()](https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#str.lower) or
[bytes.lower()](https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#bytes.lower)
method, depending on the input value type.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Convert to lower case
    ${str1} =    Convert To Lower Case    ABC
    ${str2} =    Convert To Lower Case    1A2c3D
    Should Be Equal    ${str1}    abc
    Should Be Equal    ${str2}    1a2c3d
```

If this keyword is used with bytes, only ASCII characters are lowercased.
keywords.shortdoc: Converts string to lower case.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to convert.

keywords.returnDoc: The input converted to lower case.

keywords.name: Convert To Title Case
keywords.doc:
Converts string to title case.

Titlecasing is done using the following algorithm:

- Split the string to words from whitespace characters (spaces,
  newlines, etc.).
- Exclude words that are not all lower case. This preserves,
  for example, "OK" and "iPhone".
- Exclude also words listed in the optional `exclude` argument.
- Title case the first alphabetical character of each word that has
  not been excluded.
- Join all words together so that original whitespace is preserved.

Explicitly excluded words can be given as a list or as a string with
words separated by a comma and an optional space. Excluded words are
actually considered to be regular expression patterns, so it is
possible to use something like `example[.!?]?` to match the word
`example` on its own and also if followed by `.`, `!` or `?`.
See the [BuiltIn] library keyword `Should Match Regexp` for more
information about Python regular expression syntax in general and
how to use it in Robot Framework data in particular.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Convert to title case
    ${str1} =    Convert To Title Case    hello, world!
    ${str2} =    Convert To Title Case    it's an OK iPhone    exclude=a, an, the
    ${str3} =    Convert To Title Case    distance is 1 km.    exclude=is, km.?
    Should Be Equal    ${str1}    Hello, World!
    Should Be Equal    ${str2}    It's an OK iPhone
    Should Be Equal    ${str3}    Distance is 1 km.
```

The reason this keyword does not use Python's standard
[str.title()](https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#str.title)
method is that it can yield undesired results, for example, if
strings contain upper case letters or special characters like
apostrophes. It would, for example, convert "it's an OK iPhone"
to "It'S An Ok Iphone".

If this keyword is used with bytes, only ASCII characters are titlecased.
Bytes support is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Converts string to title case.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to convert.

args.name: exclude
args.doc:
Optional words to exclude from title casing. Can be a list
or a comma-separated string. Each word is treated as a regular
expression pattern.
args.repr: exclude: str | bytes | list[str | bytes] | None = None

keywords.returnDoc: The input converted to title case.

keywords.name: Convert To Upper Case
keywords.doc:
Converts string to upper case.

Uses Python's standard
[str.upper()](https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#str.upper) or
[bytes.upper()](https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#bytes.upper)
method, depending on the input value type.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Convert to upper case
    ${str1} =    Convert To Upper Case    abc
    ${str2} =    Convert To Upper Case    1a2C3d
    Should Be Equal    ${str1}    ABC
    Should Be Equal    ${str2}    1A2C3D
```

If this keyword is used with bytes, only ASCII characters are uppercased.
keywords.shortdoc: Converts string to upper case.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to convert.

keywords.returnDoc: The input converted to upper case.

keywords.name: Decode Bytes To String
keywords.doc:
Decodes the given `bytes` to a string using the given `encoding`.

The `errors` argument supports all Python's standard
[error handlers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/codecs.html#error-handlers),
but in practice the following values are most useful:

- `strict`: fail if characters cannot be encoded (default)
- `ignore`: ignore characters that cannot be encoded
- `replace`: replace characters that cannot be encoded with
  a replacement character

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Decide bytes ti strinog
    ${string} =    Decode Bytes To String    ${bytes}    UTF-8
    ${string} =    Decode Bytes To String    ${bytes}    ASCII    errors=ignore
```

Use the [Encode String To Bytes] keyword if you need to convert strings
to bytes. Use the [BuiltIn] library keyword `Convert To String` if
you want to convert arbitrary objects to strings.
keywords.shortdoc: Decodes the given `bytes` to a string using the given `encoding`.

args.name: bytes
args.doc: The bytes to decode.

args.name: encoding
args.doc: The encoding to use.

args.name: errors
args.doc: How to handle encoding errors.

keywords.returnDoc: The input bytes decoded to string,

keywords.name: Encode String To Bytes
keywords.doc:
Encodes the given `string` to bytes using the given `encoding`.

The `errors` argument supports all Python's standard
[error handlers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/codecs.html#error-handlers),
but in practice the following values are most useful:

- `strict`: fail if characters cannot be encoded (default)
- `ignore`: ignore characters that cannot be encoded
- `replace`: replace characters that cannot be encoded with
  a replacement character

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Encode string to bytes
    ${bytes} =    Encode String To Bytes    ${string}    UTF-8
    ${bytes} =    Encode String To Bytes    ${string}    ASCII    errors=ignore
```

Use the [Decode Bytes To String] keyword if you need to convert bytes
to strings. Use the [BuiltIn] library keyword `Convert To Bytes` if
you want to create bytes based on character or integer sequences.
keywords.shortdoc: Encodes the given `string` to bytes using the given `encoding`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string to encode.

args.name: encoding
args.doc: The encoding to use.

args.name: errors
args.doc: How to handle encoding errors.

keywords.returnDoc: The input string encoded to bytes.

keywords.name: Fetch From Left
keywords.doc:
Returns contents of the `string` before the first occurrence of `marker`.

If the `marker` is not found, whole string is returned.

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

See also [Fetch From Right], [Split String] and [Split String From Right].
keywords.shortdoc: Returns contents of the `string` before the first occurrence of `marker`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to search from.

args.name: marker
args.doc: The marker string to search for.

keywords.returnDoc: The part of the string before the first `marker`.

keywords.name: Fetch From Right
keywords.doc:
Returns contents of the `string` after the last occurrence of `marker`.

If the `marker` is not found, whole string is returned.

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

See also [Fetch From Left], [Split String] and [Split String From Right].
keywords.shortdoc: Returns contents of the `string` after the last occurrence of `marker`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to search from.

args.name: marker
args.doc: The marker string to search for.

keywords.returnDoc: The part of the string after the last `marker`.

keywords.name: Format String
keywords.doc:
Formats a `template` using the given `positional` and `named` arguments.

The template can be either be a string or an absolute path to
an existing file. In the latter case the file is read and its contents
are used as the template. If the template file contains non-ASCII
characters, it must be encoded using UTF-8.

The template is formatted using Python's [format string syntax].
Placeholders are marked using `{}` with possible
field name and format specification inside. Literal curly braces
can be inserted by doubling them like `{{` and `}}`.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Format string
    ${to} =    Format String    To: {} <{}>                 ${user}    ${email}
    ${to} =    Format String    To: {name} <{email}>        name=${name}    email=${email}
    ${to} =    Format String    To: {u.name} <{u.email}>    u=${user_object}
    ${xx} =    Format String    {:*^30}                     centered
    ${yy} =    Format String    {0:{width}{base}}           ${42}    base=X    width=10
    ${zz} =    Format String    ${CURDIR}/template.txt      positional    named=value
```

Prior to Robot Framework 7.1, possible equal signs in the template string
needed to be escaped with a backslash like `x\={}`. Bytes support is new
in Robot Framework 7.4.

[format string syntax]: https://docs.python.org/library/string.html#format-string-syntax
keywords.shortdoc: Formats a `template` using the given `positional` and `named` arguments.

args.name: template
args.doc: A template string or an absolute path to a template file.

args.name: positional
args.doc: Positional arguments used to format the template.

args.name: named
args.doc: Named arguments used to format the template.

keywords.name: Generate Random String
keywords.doc:
Generates a string with a desired `length` from the given `chars`.

`length` can be given as a number, a string representation of a number,
or as a range of numbers, such as `5-10`. When a range of values is given
the range will be selected by random within the range.

The population sequence `chars` contains the characters to use
when generating the random string. It can contain any
characters, and it is possible to use special markers
explained in the table below:

|   Marker    |                   Explanation                        |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `[LOWER]`   | Lowercase ASCII characters from `a` to `z`.          |
| `[UPPER]`   | Uppercase ASCII characters from `A` to `Z`.          |
| `[LETTERS]` | Lowercase and uppercase ASCII characters.            |
| `[NUMBERS]` | Numbers from 0 to 9.                                 |
| `[ARABIC]`  | Arabic characters from U+0600 to U+06FF (inclusive). |
| `[POLISH]`  | ASCII characters and Polish diacritical signs.       |

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Generate random string
    ${ret} =    Generate Random String
    ${low} =    Generate Random String    12    [LOWER]
    ${bin} =    Generate Random String    8     01
    ${hex} =    Generate Random String    4     [NUMBERS]abcdef
    ${rnd} =    Generate Random String    5-10
```

Giving `length` as a range of values is new in Robot Framework 5.0.
Support for `[POLISH]` and `[ARABIC]` markers is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Generates a string with a desired `length` from the given `chars`.

args.name: length
args.doc:
Desired length of the generated string. Can be an integer,
a string representation of an integer, or a range like `5-10`.

args.name: chars
args.doc: Characters to use when generating the string.

keywords.name: Get Line
keywords.doc:
Returns the specified line from the given `string`.

Line numbering starts from 0, and it is possible to use
negative indices to refer to lines from the end. The line is
returned without the newline character.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Get line
    ${first} =    Get Line    ${string}    0
    ${2nd last} =    Get Line    ${string}    -2
```

Use [Split To Lines] if all lines, or a subset of lines, are needed.
keywords.shortdoc: Returns the specified line from the given `string`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to get the line from.

args.name: line_number
args.doc: Index of the line to return.

keywords.returnDoc: The specified line without the newline character.

keywords.name: Get Line Count
keywords.doc: Returns and logs the number of lines in the given string.
keywords.shortdoc: Returns and logs the number of lines in the given string.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to count lines from.

keywords.name: Get Lines Containing String
keywords.doc:
Returns lines of the given `string` that contain the `pattern`.

The `pattern` is always considered to be a normal string, not a glob
or regexp pattern. A line matches if the `pattern` is found anywhere
on it.

The match is case-sensitive by default, but that can be changed by
giving `ignore_case` a true value. This option is new in Robot
Framework 7.0, but with older versions it is possible to use the
nowadays deprecated `case_insensitive` argument.

Lines are returned as a single string with lines joined together with
a newline. Possible trailing newline is never returned. The number
of matching lines is automatically logged.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Get lines containing string
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Containing String    ${string}    An example
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Containing String    ${string}    FAIL    ignore_case=True
```

See [Get Lines Matching Pattern] and [Get Lines Matching Regexp]
if you need more complex pattern matching.

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. Bytes support is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Returns lines of the given `string` that contain the `pattern`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to search lines from.

args.name: pattern
args.doc: The string pattern to search for.

args.name: case_insensitive
args.doc: Deprecated alias for `ignore_case`.

args.name: ignore_case
args.doc: If given a true value, matching is case-insensitive.

keywords.name: Get Lines Matching Pattern
keywords.doc:
Returns lines of the given `string` that match the `pattern`.

The `pattern` is a _glob pattern_ where:

|   Pattern  |                    Meaning                        |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `*`        | Matches everything.                               |
| `?`        | Matches any single character.                     |
| `[chars]`  | Matches any character inside square brackets (e.g. `[abc]` matches either `a`, `b` or `c`). |
| `[!chars]` | Matches any character not inside square brackets. |

A line matches only if it matches the `pattern` fully.

The match is case-sensitive by default, but that can be changed by
giving `ignore_case` a true value. This option is new in Robot
Framework 7.0, but with older versions it is possible to use the
nowadays deprecated `case_insensitive` argument.

Lines are returned as a single string with lines joined together with
a newline. Possible trailing newline is never returned. The number
of matching lines is automatically logged.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Get lines matching regexp
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Matching Pattern    ${string}    Wild???? example
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Matching Pattern    ${string}    FAIL: *    ignore_case=True
```

See [Get Lines Matching Regexp] if you need more complex
patterns and [Get Lines Containing String] if searching
literal strings is enough.

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. Bytes support is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Returns lines of the given `string` that match the `pattern`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to search lines from.

args.name: pattern
args.doc: The glob pattern to match.

args.name: case_insensitive
args.doc: Deprecated alias for `ignore_case`.

args.name: ignore_case
args.doc: If given a true value, matching is case-insensitive.

keywords.name: Get Lines Matching Regexp
keywords.doc:
Returns lines of the given `string` that match the regexp `pattern`.

Lines match only if they match the pattern fully by default, but
partial matching can be enabled by giving the `partial_match`
argument a true value.

If the pattern is empty, it matches only empty lines by default.
When partial matching is enabled, empty pattern matches all lines.

Possible flags altering how the expression is parsed (e.g. `re.IGNORECASE`,
`re.VERBOSE`) can be given using the `flags` argument (e.g.
`flags=IGNORECASE | VERBOSE`) or embedded to the pattern (e.g.
`(?ix)pattern`).

Lines are returned as a single string concatenated back together with
newlines. Possible trailing newline is never returned. The
number of matching lines is automatically logged.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Get lines matching regexp
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Matching Regexp    ${string}    Reg\\w{3} example
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Matching Regexp    ${string}    Reg\\w{3} example    partial_match=True
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Matching Regexp    ${string}    (?i)FAIL: .*
    ${lines} =    Get Lines Matching Regexp    ${string}    FAIL: .*    flags=IGNORECASE
```

Notice that the backslash character that is often used with regular
expressions is an escape character in Robot Framework data. If
a literal backslash is needed, it needs to be doubled as the above
example illustrates. For more information about the supported regular
expression syntax and using regular expressions with Robot Framework
in general, see the documentation of the [BuiltIn] library keyword
`Should Match Regexp` keyword.

Use [Get Lines Matching Pattern] and [Get Lines Containing String] if
you do not need the full regular expression powers (and complexity).

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

The `flags` argument is new in Robot Framework 6.0.
keywords.shortdoc: Returns lines of the given `string` that match the regexp `pattern`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to search lines from.

args.name: pattern
args.doc: The regular expression pattern to match.

args.name: partial_match
args.doc:
If given a true value, lines match if the pattern
is found anywhere on the line.

args.name: flags
args.doc: Optional regular expression flags.

keywords.name: Get Regexp Matches
keywords.doc:
Returns a list of all non-overlapping matches in the given string.

`string` is the string to find matches from and `pattern` is the
regular expression. See the [BuiltIn] library keyword `Should Match Regexp`
for more information about Python regular expression syntax in general
and how to use it in Robot Framework data in particular.

If no groups are used, the returned list contains full matches. If one
group is used, the list contains only contents of that group. If
multiple groups are used, the list contains tuples that contain
individual group contents. All groups can be given as indexes (starting
from 1) and named groups can also be given as names.

Possible flags altering how the expression is parsed (e.g. `re.IGNORECASE`,
`re.MULTILINE`) can be given using the `flags` argument (e.g.
`flags=IGNORECASE | MULTILINE`) or embedded to the pattern (e.g.
`(?im)pattern`).

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Variables ***
${string}        the string

*** Test Cases ***
No match
    ${result} =    Get Regexp Matches    ${string}    xxx
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    []    type=list

Match
    ${result} =    Get Regexp Matches    ${string}    t..
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    ["the", "tri"]    type=list

Flags
    ${result} =    Get Regexp Matches    ${string}    T..    flags=IGNORECASE
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    ["the", "tri"]    type=list

One group by index
    ${result} =    Get Regexp Matches    ${string}    t(..)    1
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    ["he", "ri"]    type=list

One group by name
    ${result} =    Get Regexp Matches    ${string}    t(?P<name>..)    name
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    ["he", "ri"]    type=list

Multiple groups
    ${result} =    Get Regexp Matches    ${string}    t(.)(.)    1    2
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    [("h", "e"), ("r", "i")]    type=list
```

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

The `flags` argument is new in Robot Framework 6.0.
keywords.shortdoc: Returns a list of all non-overlapping matches in the given string.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to find matches from.

args.name: pattern
args.doc: The regular expression pattern to match.

args.name: groups
args.doc: Optional group indexes or names to return.

args.name: flags
args.doc: Optional regular expression flags.

keywords.returnDoc: A list of matches, group contents, or tuples of group contents.

keywords.name: Get Substring
keywords.doc:
Returns a substring from `start` index to `end` index.

The `start` index is inclusive and `end` is exclusive.
Indexing starts from 0, and it is possible to use
negative indices to refer to characters from the end.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Get substring
    ${ignore first} =    Get Substring    ${string}    1
    ${ignore last} =     Get Substring    ${string}    0    -1
    ${5th to 10th} =     Get Substring    ${string}    4    10
    ${first two} =       Get Substring    ${string}    end=1
    ${last two} =        Get Substring    ${string}    -2
```

Default value with `start` is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Returns a substring from `start` index to `end` index.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to get the substring from.

args.name: start
args.doc: Start index. Defaults to `0`.

args.name: end
args.doc: End index. Defaults to `None` (end of string).

keywords.name: Remove String
keywords.doc:
Removes all `removables` from the given `string`.

`removables` are used as literal strings. Each removable will be
matched to a temporary string from which preceding removables have
been already removed. See the second example below.

Use [Remove String Using Regexp] if more powerful pattern matching is
needed. If only a certain number of matches should be removed,
[Replace String] or [Replace String Using Regexp] can be used.

A modified version of the string is returned and the original
string is not altered.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Remove string
    ${str} =    Remove String    Robot Framework    work
    Should Be Equal    ${str}    Robot Frame
    ${str} =    Remove String    Robot Framework    o    bt
    Should Be Equal    ${str}    R Framewrk
```

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. Bytes support is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Removes all `removables` from the given `string`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to modify.

args.name: removables
args.doc: Strings to remove.

keywords.name: Remove String Using Regexp
keywords.doc:
Removes `patterns` from the given `string`.

This keyword is otherwise identical to [Remove String], but
the `patterns` to search for are considered to be a regular
expression. See [Replace String Using Regexp] for more information
about the regular expression syntax. That keyword can also be
used if there is a need to remove only a certain number of
occurrences.

Possible flags altering how the expression is parsed (e.g. `re.IGNORECASE`,
`re.MULTILINE`) can be given using the `flags` argument (e.g.
`flags=IGNORECASE | MULTILINE`) or embedded to the pattern (e.g.
`(?im)pattern`).

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. Bytes support is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

The `flags` argument is new in Robot Framework 6.0.
keywords.shortdoc: Removes `patterns` from the given `string`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to modify.

args.name: patterns
args.doc: Regular expression patterns to remove.

args.name: flags
args.doc: Optional regular expression flags.

keywords.name: Replace String
keywords.doc:
Replaces `search_for` in the given `string` with `replace_with`.

If the optional argument `count` is given, only that many
occurrences from left are replaced. Negative `count` means
that all occurrences are replaced (default behavior) and zero
means that nothing is done.

`search_for` is used as a literal string. See [Replace String
Using Regexp] if more powerful pattern matching is needed.
If you need to just remove a string, see [Remove String].

A modified version of the string is returned and the original
string is not altered.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Replace string
    ${str} =    Replace String    Hello, world!    world    tellus
    Should Be Equal    ${str}    Hello, tellus!
    ${str} =    Replace String    Hello, world!    l    e    count=1
    Should Be Equal    ${str}    Heelo, world!
```

If the first argument is bytes, the following two arguments are automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Replaces `search_for` in the given `string` with `replace_with`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to modify.

args.name: search_for
args.doc: The string to search for.

args.name: replace_with
args.doc: The replacement string.

args.name: count
args.doc: Maximum number of replacements. `-1` means all (default).

keywords.name: Replace String Using Regexp
keywords.doc:
Replaces `pattern` in the given `string` with `replace_with`.

This keyword is otherwise identical to [Replace String], but
the `pattern` to search for is considered to be a regular
expression.  See the [BuiltIn] library keyword `Should Match Regexp`
for more information about Python regular expression syntax in general
and how to use it in Robot Framework data in particular.

Possible flags altering how the expression is parsed (e.g. `re.IGNORECASE`,
`re.MULTILINE`) can be given using the `flags` argument (e.g.
`flags=IGNORECASE | MULTILINE`) or embedded to the pattern (e.g.
`(?im)pattern`).

If you need to just remove a string see [Remove String Using Regexp].

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Replace string using regexp
    ${str} =    Replace String Using Regexp    ${str}    2026-\\d\\d-\\d\\d    <DATE>
    ${str} =    Replace String Using Regexp    ${str}    (Hello|Hi)    Moi    count=1
```

If the first argument is bytes, the following two arguments are automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

The `flags` argument is new in Robot Framework 6.0.
keywords.shortdoc: Replaces `pattern` in the given `string` with `replace_with`.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to modify.

args.name: pattern
args.doc: The regular expression pattern to search for.

args.name: replace_with
args.doc: The replacement string.

args.name: count
args.doc: Maximum number of replacements. `-1` means all (default).

args.name: flags
args.doc: Optional regular expression flags.

keywords.name: Should Be Byte String
keywords.doc:
Fails if the given `item` is not a byte string.

Use [Should Be String] if you want to verify the `item` is a string.
keywords.shortdoc: Fails if the given `item` is not a byte string.

args.name: item

keywords.name: Should Be Title Case
keywords.doc:
Fails if given `string` is not title.

`string` is a title cased string if there is at least one upper case
letter in each word.

For example, `'This Is Title'` and `'OK, Give Me My iPhone'`
would pass. `'all words lower'` and `'Word In lower'` would fail.

This logic changed in Robot Framework 4.0 to be compatible with
[Convert To Title Case]. See [Convert To Title Case] for title case
algorithm and reasoning.

See also [Should Be Upper Case] and [Should Be Lower Case].

keywords.name: Split String
keywords.doc:
Splits the `string` using `separator` as a delimiter string.

If a `separator` is not given, any whitespace string is a
separator. In that case also possible consecutive whitespace
as well as leading and trailing whitespace is ignored.

Split parts are returned as a list. If the optional
`max_split` is given, at most `max_split` splits are done, and
the returned list will have maximum `max_split + 1` elements.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Split string
    @{words} =    Split String    ${string}
    @{words} =    Split String    ${string}    ,${SPACE}
    ${pre}    ${post} =    Split String    ${string}    ::    1
```

See [Split String From Right] if you want to start splitting
from right, and [Fetch From Left] and [Fetch From Right] if
you only want to get first/last part of the string.

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Splits the `string` using `separator` as a delimiter string.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to split.

args.name: separator
args.doc: The delimiter string. Defaults to splitting on whitespace.

args.name: max_split
args.doc: Maximum number of splits. `-1` means no limit (default).

keywords.name: Split String From Right
keywords.doc:
Splits the `string` using `separator` starting from right.

Same as [Split String], but splitting is started from right. This has
an effect only when `max_split` is given.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Split string from right
    ${first}    ${rest} =    Split String    ${string}    -    1
    ${rest}    ${last} =    Split String From Right    ${string}    -    1
```

If the first argument is bytes, the second argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. This is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Splits the `string` using `separator` starting from right.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to split.

args.name: separator
args.doc: The delimiter string. Defaults to splitting on whitespace.

args.name: max_split
args.doc: Maximum number of splits. `-1` means no limit (default).

keywords.name: Split String To Characters
keywords.doc:
Splits the given `string` to characters.

Example:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Split string to characters
    @{characters} =    Split String To Characters    ${string}
```

Bytes support is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Splits the given `string` to characters.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to split.

keywords.returnDoc: A list of single-character strings or bytes.

keywords.name: Split To Lines
keywords.doc:
Splits the given string to lines.

It is possible to get only a selection of lines from `start`
to `end` so that `start` index is inclusive and `end` is
exclusive. Line numbering starts from 0, and it is possible to
use negative indices to refer to lines from the end.

Lines are returned without the newlines. The number of
returned lines is automatically logged.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Split to lines
    @{lines} =           Split To Lines    ${string}
    @{ignore first} =    Split To Lines    ${string}    1
    @{ignore last} =     Split To Lines    ${string}    end=-1
    @{5th to 10th} =     Split To Lines    ${string}    4    10
    @{first two} =       Split To Lines    ${string}    end=1
    @{last two} =        Split To Lines    ${string}    start=-2
```

Use [Get Line] if you only need to get a single line.
keywords.shortdoc: Splits the given string to lines.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to split.

args.name: start
args.doc: Start index for line selection. Defaults to `0`.

args.name: end
args.doc: End index for line selection. Defaults to `None` (end of string).

keywords.name: Strip String
keywords.doc:
Remove leading and/or trailing whitespaces from the given string.

`mode` is either `left` to remove leading characters, `right` to
remove trailing characters, `both` (default) to remove the
characters from both sides of the string or `none` to return the
unmodified string.

This keyword strips whitespace by default, but arbitrary characters
can be stripped by using the optional `characters` argument.
As the example below illustrates, each character is separately stripped
instead of considering `characters` a substring to be stripped.

Examples:

```robotframework
*** Test Cases ***
Strip string
    ${stripped} =    Strip String    ${SPACE}Hello${SPACE}
    Should Be Equal    ${stripped}    Hello
    ${stripped} =    Strip String    ${SPACE}Hello${SPACE}    mode=left
    Should Be Equal    ${stripped}    Hello${SPACE}
    ${stripped} =    Strip String    aabaHelloeee    characters=abe
    Should Be Equal    ${stripped}    Hello
```

If the first argument is bytes, the `characters` argument is automatically
converted to bytes as well. Bytes support is new in Robot Framework 7.4.
keywords.shortdoc: Remove leading and/or trailing whitespaces from the given string.

args.name: string
args.doc: The string or bytes to strip.

args.name: mode
args.doc: Which end(s) of the string to strip from.

args.name: characters
args.doc: Optional characters to remove instead of whitespace.

typedocs.name: boolean
typedocs.doc:
Strings `TRUE`, `YES`, `ON`, `1` and possible localization specific "true strings"
are converted to Boolean `True`, the empty string, strings `FALSE`, `NO`, `OFF`
and `0` and possibly localization specific "false strings" are converted to
Boolean `False`, and the string `NONE` is converted to the Python `None` object.
Other strings and all other values are passed as-is, allowing keywords to handle
them specially if needed.

All string comparisons are case-insensitive.

Examples: `TRUE` (converted to `True`), `off` (converted to `False`), `example`
(used as-is)

typedocs.name: bytes
typedocs.doc:
Strings are converted to bytes so that each Unicode code point below 256 is
directly mapped to a matching byte. Higher code points are not allowed.
Robot Framework's `\xHH` escape syntax is convenient with bytes having
non-printable values.

Examples: `good`, `hyvä` (same as `hyv\xE4`), `\x00` (the null byte)

Integers and sequences of integers are converted to matching bytes directly.
They must be in range 0-255.

Examples: `0` (converted to the null byte), `[82, 70]` (converted to `RF`)

Support for integers and sequences of integers is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

typedocs.name: integer
typedocs.doc:
Conversion is done using Python's [int] built-in function. Floating point numbers
are accepted only if they can be represented as integers exactly. For example,
`1.0` is accepted but `1.1` is not.

It is possible to use hexadecimal, octal and binary numbers by prefixing values
with `0x`, `0o` and `0b`, respectively.

Spaces and underscores can be used as visual separators for digit grouping purposes.

Examples: `42`, `-1`, `0b1010`, `10 000 000`, `0xBAD_C0FFEE`

[int]: https://docs.python.org/library/functions.html#int

typedocs.name: list
typedocs.doc:
Strings must be Python [list] or [tuple] literals. They are converted using the
[ast.literal_eval] function and possible tuples are converted further to lists.
They can contain any values `ast.literal_eval` supports, including lists and
other collections.

If the argument is a list, it is used without conversion. Tuples and other
sequences are converted to lists.

If the type has nested types like `list[int]`, items are converted to those
types automatically.

Examples: `['one', 'two']`, `[('one', 1), ('two', 2)]`

Support to convert nested types is new in Robot Framework 6.0. Support for tuple
literals is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

[list]: https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#list
[tuple]: https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#tuple
[ast.literal_eval]: https://docs.python.org/library/stdtypes.html#ast.literal_eval

typedocs.name: Literal
typedocs.doc:
Only specified values are accepted. Values can be strings, integers, bytes,
Booleans, enums and None, and used arguments are converted using the value type
specific conversion logic.

String matching is case, space, underscore and hyphen insensitive, but exact
matches have precedence over normalized matches.

typedocs.name: None
typedocs.doc:
String `NONE` (case-insensitive) and the empty string are converted to the Python
`None` object. Other values cause an error.

Converting the empty string is new in Robot Framework 7.4.

typedocs.name: object
typedocs.doc: Any value is accepted. No conversion is done.

typedocs.name: string
typedocs.doc:
All arguments are converted to Unicode strings.

Most values are converted simply by using `str(value)`. An exception is that
bytes are mapped directly to Unicode code points with same ordinals. This means
that, for example, `b"hyv\xe4"` becomes `"hyvä"`.

Converting bytes specially is new Robot Framework 7.4.
